neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented. Normal cognition. Mild fatigue.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Right ptosis, moderate — levator excursion 7mm (left 12mm). Fatigable ptosis right eye on sustained upgaze at 45 seconds. Diplopia on rightward gaze. Limited right eye abduction. Pupils equal, reactive. Facial weakness bilateral. Voice nasal after prolonged speech.
neurological_exam.motor: Deltoids 4/5 bilaterally. Hip flexors 4+/5. Neck flexors 4/5. Distal strength 5/5. Fatigability documented.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal casual. Mildly slow on prolonged walking.
neurological_exam.additional: NIF -54 cmH2O. Mild dysphagia — food sticks. Anti-titin ordered as part of initial workup.

patient.chief_complaint: Drooping right eyelid and double vision worsening over 6 months
patient.history_present_illness: A 62-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hypothyroidism presented for neurological evaluation of progressive right eyelid drooping and double vision over 6 months. He first noticed intermittent right eyelid drooping approximately 6 months ago, occurring mainly after a full day of work. He is a high school principal and noted the drooping was worst during late-afternoon meetings. Over 3 months, the ptosis became more persistent and began appearing in the morning as well, though it was consistently worse by afternoon. He developed horizontal double vision on looking to the right about 4 months ago. He describes the images as side by side, one in front of the other when looking to the right. He found himself instinctively turning his head to the right to avoid diplopia. Over the past 6 weeks, he has had increasing difficulty chewing steaks and other tough foods — he used to enjoy a steak dinner with his wife on Fridays but has stopped because his jaw gives out after a few bites. He also notices that his voice becomes nasal and harder to understand during long faculty meetings and he has had to shorten his public speaking. He denies sensory symptoms, no limb weakness at rest, no headache, no visual blurring beyond the diplopia. He had a brain MRI performed by his primary care physician that was reported as showing 'mild white matter changes, age-appropriate,' which was reassuring but did not explain his symptoms. His diabetes is well-controlled (HbA1c 6.9%) and his levothyroxine is adequate (TSH 1.4). He has no family history of neuromuscular disease.

findings.significance: Normal motor and sensory conduction; normal baseline CMAP amplitudes

specialized_test.impression: Clearly abnormal RNS with 16–21% decremental responses across deltoid, nasalis, and masseter muscles. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission

labs.interpretation: Anti-AChR binding antibody markedly elevated at 6.4 nmol/L (reference <0.5 nmol/L). Anti-AChR blocking and modulating antibodies also elevated. Anti-MuSK negative. Anti-titin antibody positive. Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies are found in a subset of patients with neuromuscular junction disorders; elevated results are associated with autoimmune neuromuscular junction disease
abnormal_values_summary: Anti-AChR binding 6.4 nmol/L (markedly elevated; ref <0.5 nmol/L)

findings.description: Anterior mediastinal mass with heterogeneous enhancement. Lobulated. No clear vascular invasion. No lymphadenopathy.

ct.impression: Anterior mediastinal mass measuring 3.6 x 2.9 cm with heterogeneous soft tissue enhancement. Lobulated margins. No mediastinal lymphadenopathy. No pleural effusion. Lungs clear

output.impression: Markedly abnormal SFEMG with increased jitter (mean MCD 74 µs) and high blocking rate (70%). Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission

findings.description: Well-circumscribed encapsulated anterior mediastinal mass. No invasion.

output.impression: Well-circumscribed anterior mediastinal mass 3.6 x 2.9 x 3.1 cm with soft tissue density. Encapsulated appearance. No evidence of pleural involvement or lymphadenopathy on this examination

output.proposed: Pyridostigmine 60mg q4-6h for MG in patient on metoprolol succinate 50mg
interactions: Pyridostigmine + metoprolol: both can have additive bradycardic effects; cholinergic stimulation from pyridostigmine increases vagal tone; metoprolol is beta-blocker — bradycardia risk
Clinical significance: monitor heart rate closely; typical pyridostigmine doses well tolerated with metoprolol at standard doses
warnings: Monitor resting heart rate — hold pyridostigmine if HR <50
Baseline ECG recommended before pyridostigmine initiation
Glycopyrrolate or atropine available in event of symptomatic bradycardia

output.proposed: Prednisone for MG in patient with well-controlled T2DM on metformin (HbA1c 6.9%)
interactions: Prednisone + metformin: corticosteroids antagonize insulin and cause hyperglycemia; metformin will be insufficient for steroid-induced glucose rise
Expected glucose increase: 40-60 mg/dL with prednisone 15-20 mg/day
warnings: Monitor blood glucose closely — 4x daily monitoring during prednisone initiation
May need to add basal insulin (glargine) for steroid-induced hyperglycemia
HbA1c 6.9% is at target — protect glycemic control during steroid treatment
Prefer azathioprine as steroid-sparing agent to minimize prednisone duration
alternatives: Azathioprine 50mg titrating to 2-3mg/kg — preferred steroid-sparing agent

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Myasthenia gravis, generalized (MGFA Class IIb), AChR antibody-positive, with thymoma (3.6 cm anterior mediastinal mass)

differential.key_features: Diabetic cranial mononeuropathy is acute, painful, monocular; this is bilateral, fluctuating, fatigable.
Treated hypothyroidism; no fixed weakness pattern; fatigable bulbar weakness is MG.
Anti-VGCC negative; baseline CMAPs normal; AChR markedly positive.
Fluctuating fatigable pattern over months is incompatible with vascular event.
No long-tract signs; no cervical cord disease on imaging.

optimal_actions.action: Order serologies: anti-AChR (binding, blocking, modulating), anti-MuSK, anti-LRP4, and TSH/free-T4 for thyroid autoimmunity
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AChR antibody positive; TSH evaluates for comorbid thyroid disease

optimal_actions.action: Order repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) at 2-3 Hz across proximal and facial muscles
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Decrement >10% in symptomatic muscles supports postsynaptic NMJ disorder
Increased jitter and blocking on extensor digitorum communis or orbicularis oculi confirms NMJ transmission failure

optimal_actions.action: Order CT chest with contrast for thymoma screening
Review MGFA classification and current treatment guidance (pyridostigmine, prednisone, steroid-sparing, IVIG/PLEX, thymectomy)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MGFA classification stages disease severity; thymectomy benefits AChR+ generalized MG (MGTX); IVIG/PLEX for crisis

tool_parameters.query: myasthenia gravis MGFA classification treatment thymectomy

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions for MG-exacerbating agents (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, neuromuscular blockers, procainamide)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Flag aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, IV magnesium, telithromycin, NMBs as contraindicated or use-with-caution in MG

optimal_actions.action: Bedside respiratory function testing (FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF) — repeat q4h in crisis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline FVC/NIF to assess crisis risk in patients with bulbar or limb involvement

optimal_actions.action: Bedside ice-pack test for ptosis (cheap, ~80% sensitive for ocular MG)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Improvement of ptosis after 2 minutes of cooling supports MG

useless_tools.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Brain MRI is non-contributory in typical MG; reserve for cases where an alternative CNS cause (brainstem lesion, demyelination) is genuinely in the differential.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

sequence_constraints.reason: Order AChR/MuSK/LRP4 serologies first; reserve single-fiber EMG for seronegative or RNS-non-diagnostic cases (resource stewardship).

critical_actions: Confirm markedly positive AChR antibodies; anti-titin positive supports thymoma
CT chest — 3.6 cm thymoma identified; thoracic surgery referral
Pre-thymectomy MG optimization: pyridostigmine + IVIG or PLEX bridge
Pre-operative respiratory function and cardiac assessment given age and diabetes
Optimize diabetes management prior to high-dose steroids
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
key_reasoning_points: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
Anti-titin or anti-RyR antibodies in an MG patient strongly predict thymoma — CT chest is mandatory and surgical referral is non-negotiable.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute ocular symptoms to diabetic cranial neuropathy.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Diabetic cranial mononeuropathy is acute, painful, and monocular; this presentation is bilateral, fluctuating, fatigable, and AChR-antibody positive.
